To deride someone or something means to mock them or ridicule them in a way that shows you think they are stupid, worthless, or not worth taking seriously. It is not just laughing with someone — it is laughing at them, often with contempt or scorn.

When you deride something, you are doing two things at once: you are making fun of it, and you are signalling that you think it deserves no respect.

The critics derided his painting as the work of an amateur.

Here, the critics didn't simply dislike the painting — they mocked it in a way that dismissed it entirely.
What Makes "Deride" Different From Just "Making Fun"

This is the key to truly understanding the word. Not all mockery is derision. Consider the difference:

  • When friends tease each other, it is usually light, harmless, and affectionate.
  • When someone mocks another person, it is unkind but can sometimes be playful.
  • When someone derides something, the tone is cold, dismissive, and contemptuous. There is a strong sense of superiority — the person deriding feels they are far above whatever they are mocking.

Derision carries a sense of looking down on something. It is mockery with an edge of arrogance or disdain attached to it.

Imagine a scientist presenting a new theory. Some in the audience roll their eyes, laugh scornfully, and make comments like, "This is ridiculous. How could anyone take this seriously?" — they are deriding the scientist. They are not just disagreeing; they are treating the idea as so foolish that it barely deserves acknowledgment.

That dismissive, superior, scornful laughter is the heart of what deride means.

"Deride" is a transitive verb, which means it always acts on an object — you always deride someone or something.

Common sentence patterns:

  • Deride someone/something: She derided his efforts to learn the piano.
  • Deride someone/something as [something]: The plan was derided as completely unrealistic. (This pattern is very common — you mock something and label it with something dismissive.)
  • Deride someone/something for [something]: He was derided for his old-fashioned views.

"Deride" is a fairly strong word. It sits in formal to semi-formal language — you are more likely to encounter it in writing, journalism, speeches, and literature than in casual conversation. In everyday speech, people tend to say "mock," "make fun of," or "laugh at" instead.

In terms of intensity, think of it on a scale:

Tease → Mock → Ridicule → Deride → Scorn

"Deride" sits firmly on the stronger end of this spectrum. It always implies a degree of contempt — not just humor.
Related Word Forms You Will Encounter

Since you'll meet this word's family in the wild, it helps to know them:

  • Derision (noun) — the act of deriding, or the mockery itself. "He was met with derision when he proposed the idea."
  • Derisive (adjective) — describes something that expresses mockery and contempt. "She gave a derisive laugh."
  • Derisively (adverb) — in a mocking, contemptuous way. "'Oh, brilliant idea,' he said derisively."
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Ridicule — very close to deride. Slightly more general; can be done in a lighthearted way, though rarely. "Deride" almost always carries contempt.
  • Scoff at — to dismiss something as foolish, often verbally. Similar, but "scoff" emphasises the dismissal more than the mockery.
  • Jeer — to shout or call out in a mocking way, often in a crowd. More aggressive and loud than "deride."
  • Sneer at — to show contempt through facial expression or tone. More personal and quiet than "deride."
  • Mock — the broadest synonym. Milder than "deride" and doesn't always imply contempt.
• Praise, commend, admire, applaud, laud, extol — all mean to speak highly of someone or something, the complete opposite of deriding them.
One Sentence to Lock It In

If you want one sentence to anchor the meaning in your memory forever:

To deride is to mock something with contempt — not just to laugh at it, but to dismiss it as beneath respect.
